0.title: Learners of Jesus
0.essay:
Some people think of a disciple as a special kind of Christian: the keen ones, the ones on the course, the ones who seem to have it all together. The New Testament knows nothing of that. If you trust Jesus, you are his disciple. The only question is what kind of disciple you will be.

The first name

Before followers of Jesus were called Christians, they were called disciples. Luke tells us exactly when the newer name arrived: “And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians” (Acts 11:26). The two words describe the same people, and “disciple” is the word the New Testament uses for them hundreds of times. In Acts a woman in Joppa who sewed clothes for widows is simply “a disciple named Tabitha” (Acts 9:36). Not a leader, not a missionary. A disciple, like all the rest.

So discipleship is not an advanced class for the spiritually ambitious. It is ordinary Christian life seen from one angle: the angle of a learner walking behind a Master, becoming like him, and bringing others along.

Where we are going

The entry Disciple in the Theological Dictionary explains the word itself: a learner attached to a teacher, whose goal is to become like him. This study builds on that and goes further. We will look at the call to be with Jesus, the cost of following, learning that leads to obedience, growing into his likeness, following together, and helping others follow.

Some ground is covered elsewhere. New Believer’s Foundations deals with first steps, assurance, prayer, the Bible and baptism; Spiritual Disciplines with the habits through which God feeds the soul; Union with Christ with what it means to be joined to him; and Missions & the Nations with the worldwide task. This study keeps its eye on the everyday shape of following Jesus.

The chapters

Come, Follow Me; Counting the Cost; Learners Who Obey; Becoming Like the Teacher; Disciples Together; and Go and Make Disciples.

For reflection

When you hear the word “disciple”, do you think of yourself, or of someone more serious than you? What difference would it make to see your ordinary week as the life of a disciple?

1.title: Come, Follow Me
1.essay:
Discipleship does not begin with our decision to try harder. It begins with a voice by a lake, calling people by name. Before it is a programme, a course or a set of habits, it is a relationship with a living Lord who wants us with him.

He called, and they came

Mark tells the story in a few plain lines. Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee and saw two fishermen at work. “And Jesus said to them, ‘Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men’” (Mark 1:17). A little further on he saw James and John mending nets, “And immediately he called them” (Mark 1:20). Later he passed a tax booth and said to the man sitting there, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him (Mark 2:14).

Notice who moves first. The fishermen were not looking for a rabbi. Levi was not looking for anything except his next payment. Jesus came to them. Rabbis in those days were usually chosen by their students; this Rabbi chose his: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16).

That is the order of the gospel. Grace comes first. He calls; we come. Even our coming is his gift, for no one would come unless he drew them. So no disciple can boast about being a disciple. We did not earn our place in his company. We were invited, and the invitation was a kindness we did not deserve.

Look at who he called

Jesus did not pick the impressive: fishermen, a tax collector who worked for the occupying power, a political zealot, men who argued about which of them was the greatest. When Peter first saw who Jesus was, he fell at his knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). Jesus did not depart. He said, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5:10).

When the religious leaders complained that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, he answered, “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). The call to follow is not a reward for good people. It is a summons to people who know they need a physician.

So that they might be with him

Why did Jesus choose the twelve? Mark gives two reasons, and the order matters. He appointed them “so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). Being with him came before being sent by him. Before they did anything for Jesus, they spent time with Jesus. They walked the roads with him, watched him pray and saw how he treated a leper, a widow and a Roman officer.

John records the very first meeting. Two of John the Baptist’s disciples began to follow Jesus. He turned and asked, “What are you seeking?” They asked where he was staying. “He said to them, ‘Come and you will see.’ So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day” (John 1:38–39). That is how discipleship began: not with a lecture, but with an invitation to spend the day with him.

Years later, when Peter and John stood before the council in Jerusalem, their accusers were puzzled. These were “uneducated, common men”, yet they spoke with such boldness. Then the penny dropped: “they recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13). Their time with him had marked them.

Friends, not only servants

We are not with Jesus in the same way the twelve were. He has ascended to the Father. But he is no less present and no less personal. By his Spirit he dwells in his people, speaks through his word and meets us in prayer. And he describes the relationship in astonishingly warm terms: “No longer do I call you servants … but I have called you friends” (John 15:15).

It is easy to turn discipleship into a list: read this, attend that, complete the course. The study Spiritual Disciplines shows how God uses such means. But they are not the goal. The goal is Christ himself. A disciple is not someone who has completed a programme. A disciple is someone who is with Jesus and wants to stay with him.

When many turned away from Jesus, he asked the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?” Peter’s answer is the heart of every true disciple: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:67–68). We follow because we have found no one else worth following. He has the words of life. He is the life.

An example

A retired bus driver became a Christian at seventy. He worried that it was too late to be a “proper” disciple. He could not read well and had never been to Bible college. His pastor told him that the first disciples were working men too, and that Jesus’ first call to them was simply to be with him. So each morning he sat with a cup of tea, listened to a chapter of a Gospel on his phone, and talked to Jesus about it as he would to a friend. “I’m not on a course,” he told his grandson. “I’m getting to know him.”

For reflection

Do you think of your Christian life more as a relationship or as a programme? How does it change things to know that Jesus called you before you came to him? What helps you to “be with him” in an ordinary week? Read John 6:66–69. What would you say if Jesus asked you, “Do you want to go away as well?”

2.title: Counting the Cost
2.essay:
Jesus never hid the price of following him. He did not run a sales campaign with the hard parts in small print. He told the crowds plainly that it would cost them everything. And yet the same Jesus says that his yoke is easy. Both are true, and a disciple needs both.

Daily, and for everyone

“And he said to all, ‘If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me’” (Luke 9:23). Notice two small words in Luke’s version: “all”, for this is no call to a special few, and “daily”, for taking up the cross is not one heroic moment at conversion but the shape of every day.

In Jesus’ world a man carrying a cross was walking to his death. To take up the cross is to say a daily “no” to the self that wants to rule, and a daily “yes” to Jesus as Lord. It is not first about suffering in general, but about dying to self-rule.

Losing in order to find

Jesus gives the reason straight away: “For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:25–26). This is not a call to throw life away, but to stop clutching it. Those who cling to control and comfort lose the very life they were keeping; those who let go for Jesus’ sake find it given back, larger than before.

So self-denial in the Bible is not self-hatred. Jesus is not asking us to despise who God made us to be or to punish ourselves. He is asking us to dethrone the self that wants to be god. It is the surgeon’s knife, not the torturer’s.

Sit down and count

Luke 14 is the hardest of these passages. Great crowds were following Jesus, and he turned to them and said, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

What does “hate” mean here? It cannot mean bitterness or contempt, because the same Jesus commands us to honour our parents and to love even our enemies. Jesus is using a strong Hebrew way of speaking about preference: to love one thing so much more than another that, by comparison, the second looks like hatred. Matthew’s Gospel records the same teaching in plainer words: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Jesus must come first, above the dearest people in our lives. Those who love him first usually love their families better, not worse.

Then Jesus tells two short stories. A man starting a building project sits down first and counts the cost, “whether he has enough to complete it” (Luke 14:28). A king facing a larger army thinks hard before going to war. “So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Jesus wants honest followers, not ones who sign up on a wave of excitement and quit when it gets hard. On another road someone said, “I will follow you wherever you go”, and Jesus replied that “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:57–58). Count the cost. Following Jesus may cost you friendships, money, a career path or a comfortable reputation. For some believers today it costs their freedom or their life. (The studies Courage and The Fear of Man help with the fear such costs can bring.)

What we receive

But the cost is never the whole story. When Peter said, “See, we have left everything and followed you”, Jesus promised that no one who had left house or family for his sake would fail to “receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10:28–30). Jesus is honest to the end (“with persecutions”), but he promises a new family in the church and eternal life at the last. Paul, who lost a great deal, looked back and said he counted it all “as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

Costly, but never earning

Here we must be careful. The cost of discipleship is real, but it is never the price of salvation. Christ has already paid the full price, on his cross, for disciples who would often fail to carry theirs. We carry our cross because he carried his, not in order to make him accept us.

That is why the Jesus who says “take up your cross” also says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). A yoke still means work and direction, but this one is shaped by a gentle Master, and it fits. The heaviest burdens are the ones we choose for ourselves: proving our worth, earning our place. Jesus takes those off, and gives us his.

So a disciple counts the cost honestly and discovers, again and again, that Christ is worth it. Nothing we give up for him can compare with what he gave up for us.

An example

A young accountant was offered a promotion that came with a quiet expectation: to make certain figures look better than they were. She knew what following Jesus meant, and she turned it down. For a while it hurt, as colleagues overtook her. But her conscience was clear, and her small group at church surrounded her with prayer and practical help. Two years later she said, “It cost me something real. It didn’t cost me anything I actually needed.”

For reflection

What does taking up your cross “daily” look like in your life this week? Is there anything you love more than Jesus, which you need to put in second place? How does Matthew 10:37 help you understand Luke 14:26? Where do you need to hear Jesus’ invitation in Matthew 11:28–30, to lay down a burden that was never his?

3.title: Learners Who Obey
3.essay:
A disciple is a learner. But Jesus is not interested in learners who only collect information. He wants learners whose lives change. In his school, the test is not what you can recite but how you live on Monday morning.

Abiding in his word

To some who had just believed in him, Jesus said, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32). To abide is to stay, to make your home somewhere. A true disciple does not visit Jesus’ word now and then, like a tourist. He lives in it and lets it shape how he thinks and what he wants.

And this learning leads to freedom. We tend to think of instruction as restriction. Jesus says the opposite: his truth sets us free, from lies about God, from lies about ourselves, from habits that enslave us. The study Spiritual Disciplines explains how to read and meditate on Scripture. Here the point is simpler. A disciple is someone who keeps listening to Jesus.

Learn from me

In the invitation we saw in the last chapter, Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Notice what he invites us to learn: not only his teaching, but himself. We learn from his words, but also from his ways: how he spoke to the woman at the well, wept at a friend’s grave and prayed in Gethsemane.

And notice the kind of teacher he is. “Gentle and lowly in heart.” He is not impatient with slow learners. He does not sigh at our questions or humiliate us for getting things wrong. His disciples misunderstood him constantly, and he kept teaching them. If you feel like a slow pupil, you have the kindest Teacher there is.

Teaching them to observe

When Jesus sent his followers out to make disciples, he told them to be “teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). Not merely teaching what he commanded, but teaching people to observe it, to keep it, to do it. Christian teaching is never complete until it is lived.

James says the same with a vivid picture. “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22). Hearing without doing is like a man who “looks intently at his natural face in a mirror” and then walks away and forgets what he looks like (James 1:23–24). We can feel that we have grown because we heard a good sermon, when nothing in us has moved. James promises that the one who acts on what he hears “will be blessed in his doing” (James 1:25).

Obedience here is not a way of earning anything. It is the natural response of a learner who loves his Teacher. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). And we obey, imperfectly but truly, because we love.

The whole of life as an apprenticeship

In the ancient world a disciple was more like an apprentice than a student. An apprentice carpenter does not only attend lectures on wood. He learns at the bench, with his hands, beside the master, day after day. Following Jesus is like that. His lessons reach into every room of life.

Work. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). A disciple learns to do ordinary work well, honestly and without grumbling, because the real employer is Christ. Home. The way we speak to a spouse at the end of a long day, the patience we show a teenager, the care we give an elderly parent: these are where the lessons of the Sermon on the Mount are tested. Money. Jesus spoke about money often, because it so easily becomes a rival master. A disciple learns to give, to be content and to hold possessions lightly. Speech. “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6). A disciple learns to stop gossiping, to tell the truth, and to speak words that build up.

Paul sums it up: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Colossians 3:17). There is no area of life where Jesus is not Teacher. That is not a burden. It means that every ordinary day is a classroom with Christ in it.

Learning with an open Bible and an open heart

Good learners are teachable. The Christians in Berea “received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11). They were eager and they were careful. A disciple checks what he is told against Scripture, but he also comes to Scripture ready to be corrected.

An example

A father in his forties had been to church for years and could explain most doctrines well. A friend asked him one day, “What has Jesus been teaching you lately?” He realised he had no answer. He knew a great deal, but he could not name anything he had changed. So the two of them agreed to read a short passage each week and to ask one plain question about it: “What will I do differently because of this?” The first week it was James 1:19: being quick to hear and slow to speak with his children. It was a small thing. It was the beginning of learning to observe, not only to know.

For reflection

Is there a truth from Scripture you know well but have not yet put into practice? Which area of your life feels furthest from Jesus’ teaching: work, home, money or speech? How does knowing that Jesus is “gentle and lowly in heart” change the way you approach him as a learner? What one thing could you begin to “observe” this week?

4.title: Becoming Like the Teacher
4.essay:
The goal of discipleship is not information, or even obedience on its own. It is resemblance. Jesus intends his followers to become like him. That is a staggering promise, and it is God’s own purpose, which means it will not fail.

Like his teacher

Jesus said, “A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (Luke 6:40). The Dictionary entry notes this as the destination of discipleship. Follow the thought further: the end of the road is to love as Jesus loves, trust the Father as he trusts and serve as he serves.

That is not a vague hope. It is God’s eternal plan. “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). Before the world began, God the Father set his heart on a family who would look like his Son. Every step of a disciple’s growth is part of that plan coming true.

From one degree of glory to another

How does it happen? Paul answers: “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Three things stand out. First, we are changed by beholding: as we keep looking at Christ in the Scriptures, in worship and at the Lord’s Table, the Spirit makes us more like him. Second, the change is gradual: “from one degree of glory to another”. Third, it is the Spirit’s work. We are not sculptors working on ourselves with a chisel.

Yet the Spirit’s work does not make us passive. Paul says, “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). We work because he works. Our efforts are real, but they rest on his.

The marks of a disciple

What does likeness to Jesus look like? He named the chief mark himself. “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Not by our knowledge or busyness, but by love, the kind he showed when he washed his disciples’ feet and went to the cross. “Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34).

He named another mark too. “By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples” (John 15:8). Fruit grows on branches that stay joined to the vine: “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The fruit is the character of Christ formed in us: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). The study Union with Christ explains the vine and branches more fully. The point here is that genuine disciples, over time, show a family likeness.

Slow, and real

Most growth in Christ is slow. A tree does not get taller while you watch it. Many disciples are discouraged because they expected quick change and found the same battles returning. That is normal. Paul himself said, “Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12).

Notice the reason Paul presses on: because Christ has already made him his own. He is not pressing on to be accepted. He is pressing on because he has been. And the end is certain: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Your growth may be slow, but it is real, and the one doing it will finish it.

Failure and restoration

What about disciples who fail badly? Look at the twelve on the night of Jesus’ arrest. “And they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50). Peter, who had promised to die with him, denied him three times. If discipleship depended on our faithfulness, it would have ended in that courtyard.

But Jesus had seen it coming, and had already prayed: “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). After the resurrection he met Peter on the beach. He cooked breakfast. “Jesus said to them, ‘Come and have breakfast’” (John 21:12). Then three times, once for each denial, he asked Peter, “do you love me?” and three times gave him his work back: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). And then the words with which the whole story began: “Follow me” (John 21:19).

Here is the wonder of it. The Teacher does not expel failing pupils. He restores them and sends them out again, often more useful than before, because now they know their weakness and his grace. Peter, the denier, became the one who strengthened his brothers. “A bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:20).

An example

A woman in her fifties had followed Jesus for thirty years and still struggled with a sharp tongue. One evening she lost her temper with her sister and went to bed sure that she had made no progress at all. In the morning she happened to read an old journal from her twenties. She was startled: things she had once done without a second thought she now did not do at all, and things that had once ruled her no longer did. She still had far to go. But the Lord had been at work, quietly, all along. She confessed her harsh words, phoned her sister to apologise, and thanked God for his patience.

For reflection

In what ways can you see that the Lord has made you more like Jesus over the years? Where are you most discouraged by slow growth, and how does Philippians 1:6 speak to that? Would people who know you well recognise you as a disciple by your love? What does Jesus’ breakfast with Peter tell you about how he treats disciples who fail?

5.title: Disciples Together
5.essay:
Jesus did not call one disciple. He called twelve, and put them in a boat together. There has never been a solo disciple. We follow him in company, and part of how we grow is through one another, older and younger, teaching and being taught.

No solo disciples

Many Christians quietly assume that faith is a private matter, with church as an optional extra. The New Testament will not allow that. The first disciples learned together, failed together and were restored together. After Pentecost the new believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). Discipleship happened in community.

Paul pictures the church as a body. “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). Each member needs the others. Christ gave leaders to his church “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ … to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12–13). We grow up into Christ together, “when each part is working properly” (Ephesians 4:16). The study The Church explains why every Christian needs a local church. Here the point is that the church is the place where disciples are made and grow.

One another

Much of the New Testament’s teaching on growth is written in the plural. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom” (Colossians 3:16). “Exhort one another every day … that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). “And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24). Paul trusted ordinary believers to be “able to instruct one another” (Romans 15:14).

So discipleship is not only what the pastor does on Sunday. It happens over coffee after the service, in a home group, in a phone call to someone who has been absent. “Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17).

Older and younger

God has woven generations together for this purpose. Paul told Titus that older women “are to teach what is good, and so train the young women” (Titus 2:3–4), and that older men were to be examples too. He told Timothy to pass on what he had learned: “what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). Count the generations in that verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others also. Discipleship is a relay.

Timothy himself had been shaped long before he met Paul. His faith “dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). The study Christian Parenting explores this in the home. In the church too, younger believers need older ones who have walked further, and older ones need the younger.

Paul could say, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Discipleship is caught as well as taught. We learn how to pray, how to suffer, how to apologise and how to love by watching people who do it. Hebrews tells us to remember faithful leaders: “Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

The humility to be taught

Being discipled requires humility. “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice” (Proverbs 12:15). Apollos was a gifted preacher, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, “they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). He listened. A disciple who will not be taught has stopped being a disciple in any real sense.

So ask yourself: who is helping me follow Jesus? If the honest answer is “no one”, ask an older Christian to read the Bible with you, or join a small group.

A guard rail: never controlling

Discipling relationships are a great good, and like every good thing they can be twisted. There have been movements, sometimes called “shepherding”, in which leaders or mentors claimed authority over the private decisions of those they discipled: whom to marry, where to work, what to buy. Some have demanded obedience that overrides the conscience and isolated people from friends and family. That is not discipleship. It is abuse.

Scripture forbids it. Elders are to shepherd the flock “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). Jesus told his followers that rulers of the nations lord it over people, but “It shall not be so among you” (Matthew 20:26). Even the apostle Paul wrote, “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:24). There is one Master: “you have one teacher, and you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:8). Every human guide is a fellow disciple, accountable to Christ and to the church. Faithful leaders are to be respected and followed in what Scripture teaches (Hebrews 13:17), but no one may bind your conscience where God’s word leaves you free.

If you are in a relationship where someone controls your choices, demands secrecy, cuts you off from others or makes you afraid, please talk to someone outside it whom you trust, such as another pastor or a biblical counsellor. If there is abuse of any kind, your safety comes first, and it should be reported to the proper authorities.

An example

A young mum felt stuck in her faith. An older widow at church noticed and invited her round on Tuesday mornings while the baby napped. They read a passage of Mark together and talked about life. The older woman never told her what to do. She asked questions, told stories of her own mistakes, and prayed. A year later the young mum said that what helped most was not any single conversation but seeing how her friend trusted God when her own health began to fail.

For reflection

Who has helped you most to follow Jesus, and what did they do? Who is helping you now? Are you more ready to teach others or to be taught yourself? What signs would tell you that a discipling relationship had become unhealthy?

6.title: Go and Make Disciples
6.essay:
The last command Jesus gave on earth was not addressed to a few professionals. It was given to disciples, and through them to every disciple since: make disciples. That sounds daunting. But it is carried out mostly in ordinary places, by ordinary people, resting on an extraordinary promise.

The Great Commission is for you

On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:18–20).

The main command is “make disciples”. Going, baptising and teaching describe how it is done. The study Missions & the Nations looks at the worldwide sweep of this command, and the study Evangelism at sharing the gospel. Here we notice something simpler: the task is not only to see people converted, but to help them follow Jesus for the rest of their lives. That work belongs to the whole church. You may not need to cross an ocean to obey it, only the road, or the kitchen.

The command begins with Christ’s authority and ends with Christ’s presence. We do not make disciples by our own cleverness or energy. He has all authority, and he is with us.

Everyday disciple-making

Disciple-making is more like sharing a life than running an event. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians, “we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

With children. Parents are their children’s first disciple-makers. God told Israel to teach his words “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). The ordinary rhythm of family life is the classroom. With friends and colleagues. Andrew’s first act after meeting Jesus was to find his brother: “He brought him to Jesus” (John 1:42). Many come to Christ through a friend who prayed for them and, when the moment came, was “prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). With new believers. Someone newly converted needs a friend more than a course: someone to sit with them in church and show them how a Christian handles a bad day.

Reading the Bible with someone

One of the simplest and most fruitful ways to make disciples is to read the Bible one to one with another person. You do not need to be a theologian. Choose a Gospel, such as Mark. Meet regularly, and read a short passage aloud. Then ask three plain questions: What does this show us about Jesus? What does it show us about ourselves? What should we do about it? Pray together briefly, and arrange the next time.

The aim is not to impress, but to look at Jesus together and let him do the teaching. Paul’s goal is a good one to keep in mind: “that we may present everyone mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28). And remember who gives the growth: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

First steps

If you have never helped anyone follow Jesus, start small. Pray by name for two or three people: a child, a friend, a colleague, a newer Christian at church. Then take one step: invite someone for a meal, offer to read a Gospel with a new believer, or tell a friend honestly what Jesus means to you. Do not wait until you feel qualified; the first disciples were sent out while they still had much to learn.

A guard rail: rest, not burnout

Some keen Christians hear the Great Commission as a weight that never lifts, and feel guilty whenever they rest. That is not what Jesus intends. When his disciples came back exhausted from their mission, he said, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest … for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Disciple-makers are disciples first. The study Busy, Tired & Restless says more.

If overwork in ministry has left you in burnout or depression, with exhaustion that rest does not fix, sleeplessness, numbness or despair, please tell your pastor or a trusted friend, and seek out a biblical counsellor, through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation (for example ACBC or CCEF in the US, Biblical Counselling UK in Britain). A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, so that any bodily cause is found and treated, and will then help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. Asking for help is not a failure of faith, and if the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is not a failure of faith either. And if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, get help now: call the emergency services or a crisis line, and tell someone you trust.

I am with you always

The Great Commission ends not with a command but with a promise: “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The one who called fishermen by a lake and restored a failing disciple over breakfast has not sent us out alone. He goes with us wherever we try, clumsily, to help someone else follow him.

That is the whole story of discipleship. He calls us to be with him, makes us like him, and sends us to bring others to him, while he stays with us. It is the road home, walked in the best company there is.

An example

A warehouse supervisor had been a Christian for ten years but had never helped anyone else grow. When a young man in his team started coming to church, he offered to read Mark with him over lunch on Thursdays. Some weeks the young man asked questions the supervisor could not answer, and they looked them up together. Eighteen months later the young man was reading the Bible with a friend of his own. “I didn’t do much,” the supervisor said. “I just turned up and opened the book.”

For reflection

Who are the two or three people God has put near you whom you could help to follow Jesus? What would be one small first step with one of them? How do Christ’s authority and presence in Matthew 28:18–20 change how you feel about the task? Are you making disciples out of rest in Christ, or out of guilt and exhaustion?
